To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) HN2 induced cell cycle arrest in G2, which correlated with the inhibition of cdc kinase and accumulation of both tyrosl-phosphorylated and cyclin B, but not cdc2; (2) JLP119 cells evaded checkpoint control, continued to enter mitosis, and exhibited S phase arrest; (3) the greater susceptibility of the JLP119 cells correlated with the greater sensitivity to the cytotoxic action of HN2; (4)
nitrogen mustard (HN) induces cell cycle perturbants by interfering with cdc2 kinase in a manner that is dependent on the cell cycle phase at the time of HN treatment.

the G2 delay following HN2 treatment is due to a down-regulation in the activation of the cdc2 kinase and that the greater sensitivity of JLP119 to the cytotoxic and cell cycle effects of HN 2 is due to the inability of these cells to arrest at G2 following DNA damage.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the mechanisms by which DNA cross-linking agents interfere with the regulation of the cdc2-cyclin B complex, which is essential for G2 to M progression, and the role of cell cycle perturbation in the cytotoxic effects.
the role of DNA damage and cell cycle checkpoints in the control of cell proliferation.
the relationship between cdc2, DNA cross-link exposure and the cell cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cytotoxic effects induced by nitrogen mustard are mediated by DNA cross-linking and that the sensitivity of the cell to the cytotoxic effect is related to the ability to maintain a checkpoint control in the cell cycle.
the cell cycle responses to DNA damage are complex and depend on the cell type and cell cycle stage.
the cell cycle perturbation and the cytotoxicity induced by HN2 are not due to DNA cross-linking but are related to the ability of the cell to respond to DNA damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the G2 arrest following HN2 treatment was not a consequence of the drug's ability to induce DNA damage but rather was the result of the cell's response to DNA damage.
the G2 checkpoint in CA46 cells was triggered by HN2, which resulted in a down-regulation in cdc2 kinase and the phosphorylation of both cdc2 and its cyclin B partner.
the cytotoxic response of HN2 is determined by the balance of DNA cross-linking and checkpoint control.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ability to evade checkpoint control is a major factor determining the cytotoxicity of DNA-damaging agents.
the ability of cells to arrest in G2 is dependent upon a balance between the formation of DNA cross-links and the ability to activate MPF.
cell cycle checkpoints are highly sensitive to DNA damage and that cells that bypass these checkpoints are more sensitive to the lethal effects of DNA-damaging agents.
